title: DFS in Mapo-gu: Deep Dive Pathfinding
description: Watch DFS explore Seoul’s street graph by diving deep along one route before backtracking. This visualization highlights how DFS finds a path based on stack-based traversal and graph-theory structure.
ig_caption:
🗺️✨ Seoul (Mapo-gu) turns into a graph where intersections are nodes and streets are weighted edges. 

🔍💡 DFS (Depth-First Search) uses a LIFO stack to “go deep” along a chosen neighbor path, marking visited nodes to prevent loops. In graph terms, it’s a classic uninformed search strategy: it builds a traversal tree (or forest) by expanding the most recently discovered frontier, then backtracks when it hits dead ends. 

📍Real-map visualization note: with street networks, DFS behavior depends heavily on neighbor ordering—change the direction priority and the explored route changes, even though DFS stays the same algorithmically. 

🎬 Want the next algorithm (BFS, Dijkstra, A*)? Comment your pick and share this reel with a coding friend who loves real-world pathfinding! 🚀
fb_caption:
🚦 Seoul’s Mapo-gu as a graph: intersections become vertices and roads become edges. 

In this DFS pathfinding visualization, Depth-First Search explores by going deep first using a stack, then backtracking when it can’t proceed—exactly how graph search builds a traversal path while avoiding revisits. 

📣 Like, share, and tag someone who’s learning algorithms—what traversal order would you choose to guide DFS through the streets?
